strengths: Well-motivated technical approach: RER and VAPR clearly address specific limitations of fixed KL regularization with intuitive, complement mechanisms for fine-grained response-level control and long-term training stability

Comprehensive experimental validation: Thorough ablation studies (Tables 3-4, Fig. 3), evaluation on two major datasets with both NLG and clinical efficacy metrics, consistent improvements across datasets of different scales, and strong empirical gains (BLEU-4 +5.1%, RadGraph F1 +12.8%)

Practical and efficient design: RER and VAPR require no auxiliary components or preference data; use of pretrained LVLM reduces memory overhead and overfitting risks; marginal computational overhead (+1.9% step time, +3.9% memory)

Excellent reproducibility: Extensive implementation details, clear hyperparameter specifications, thorough supplementary material with reward justification, sensitivity studies, and promise of code release

Thoughtful empirical analysis: Well-supported justification of BLEU-4 reward through sign consistency analysis; detailed qualitative examples demonstrating clinical improvements; clear visualization of RER/VAPR mechanisms
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: RER is a straightforward entropy-based weighting scheme; periodic policy resets are known; while the combination is useful, individual components are incremental modifications of existing RL techniques

Indirect clinical optimization: BLEU-4 reward is a proxy justified through alignment rather than direct clinical metric optimization; CheXpert F1 and RadGraph F1 limitations are acknowledged but addressed through workaround rather than fundamental solution; no radiologist evaluation

Narrow scope and generalization concerns: Only evaluated on CXR report generation; unclear if approach generalizes to other medical imaging modalities or applications; heavy dependence on pretrained LVLM and disease classifier without sensitivity analysis across classifier quality variations (Table S8 shows AUC range 0.655–0.913)

Data and hyperparameter limitations: Stage 3 trained on subsampled data (10k vs 271k examples) due to computational constraints; multiple hyperparameters (β_min, β_base, β_max, M, λ) with dataset-specific tuning; no error bars, statistical significance tests, or multiple-run variance assessment

Lack of theoretical justification: Piecewise linear form (Eq. 9) is intuitive but unjustified; no convergence analysis or stability guarantees; entropy-based weighting is heuristic without principled design rationale

Absence of clinical validation: No human radiologist evaluation, which is critical for medical AI; automated metrics alone cannot fully assess clinical utility, safety, or real-world appropriateness of generated reports

Incomplete three-stage pipeline ablation: While Table 3 shows overall gains, it does not isolate value of each stage or justify necessity of specific three-stage structure versus simpler alternatives (e.g., direct SFT → RL)
Potential VAPR off-policy issues: Simultaneous reset of π_ref and π_θ could theoretically introduce sampling mismatch; claimed mitigation via π_θ_old synchronization deserves rigorous analysis
Limited environmental discussion: Extremely slow RL training (5 days/epoch), computational cost, and carbon footprint not discussed; scale reduction for Stage 3 may impact optimization quality

strengths: Well-motivated problem identification with clear articulation of limitations in fixed KL regularization and policy collapse issues
Comprehensive experimental validation with extensive ablation studies (Tables 3-4, Figure 3) and reward analysis in Appendix A
Strong and consistent empirical improvements across multiple metrics (BLEU-4: +5.1% MIMIC-CXR, +3.6% IU-Xray; RadGraph F1: +12.8%) on established benchmarks
Practical system design with minimal computational overhead (1.9% time, 3.9% memory), no learned reward model or preference data required
Detailed implementation details, hyperparameters, and promise of code release support reproducibility
Effective presentation with clear motivation and helpful visualizations
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: RER is straightforward adaptive weighting, VAPR is periodic checkpoint reset; both have precursors in prior work; main contribution is the combination which is incremental

BLEU-4 as reward is fundamentally misaligned for clinical applications; sign consistency (Psign=0.756→0.805) is insufficient evidence that linguistic metrics capture clinical quality; acknowledged variance in CheXpert F1 and reward inversion in RadGraph F1 represent fundamental design problems

Critical experimental limitation inadequately discussed: Stage 3 trained on only 10k of 271k MIMIC samples due to computational constraints; no analysis of how performance scales with full training data; subsampling of reports <30 tokens could introduce bias

Unclear contribution attribution: three-stage pipeline involves multiple design choices; Table 3 shows stages matter but doesn't isolate REVA-PO contribution; no comparison against (a) REVA-PO with standard training or (b) standard RL with same pipeline; unclear how much improvement comes from LVLM choice vs. REVA-PO

Inadequate theoretical justification: no principled argument for why reference entropy is the right signal; piecewise linear β function (Eq. 9) lacks justification with no ablation on functional form; group-dependent entropy normalization (Eq. 8) could cause instability across batch compositions; circular dependency between validation metrics and KL regularization

Missing critical ablations: no sensitivity analysis for hyperparameters (βmin, βmax, M, λ); no ablation on β weighting function alternatives; no systematic comparison with EMA-based updates beyond qualitative claims; reset period M=3 appears arbitrary

Narrow scope and questionable fit for ECCV: extremely specialized to CXR report generation with generalization to other medical reports or domains completely unclear; paper is more healthcare AI than core computer vision; ECCV focus on vision makes this work tangential to conference scope

Insufficient stability analysis: Figure 3 shows training curves but limited discussion of failure modes; unclear what happens when validation performance degrades or whether VAPR resets can cause divergence; method requires stable validation metrics which may be noisy in practice

Attribution of improvement unclear vs. LVLM choice: Qwen2.5-VL is novel in this domain relative to baselines, making it difficult to assess whether gains come from REVA-PO framework or architectural choice
Missing failure case analysis, clinical expert evaluation (though cost acknowledged), cross-dataset evaluation, and principled analysis of when/why entropy-based weighting helps

strengths: Well-motivated problem identification: clearly articulates the 'lose-lose' scenario with fixed KL coefficients in RL
Practical lightweight contributions: RER and VAPR add minimal computational overhead (1.9% time, 3.9% memory) while providing effective stabilization
Strong empirical results: achieves SOTA across both MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray with consistent improvements (BLEU-4: +5.1%, CheXpert F1: +4.5%, RadGraph F1: +12.8%)
Comprehensive experimental validation: thorough ablation studies (Tables 3-4), reward selection justification (Appendix A), and sensitivity analyses (Appendices E-F)
Effective application design: intelligent use of pretrained LVLM eliminates separate encoder training and reduces overfitting on limited medical data
Good presentation and clarity: clear visualizations (Figures 2, 3) effectively communicate mechanisms; detailed supplementary material supports reproducibility
weaknesses: Moderate algorithmic novelty: RER is essentially entropy-weighted KL scaling via piecewise linear interpolation; VAPR is periodic checkpointing with policy reset—both are straightforward heuristics lacking theoretical justification or convergence analysis

Fundamental mismatch in reward signal: using BLEU-4 (linguistic n-gram overlap) as the RL objective for a clinical application is conceptually problematic; justification only appears in appendix; policy collapse with CheXpert F1 suggests deeper issues with RL formulation rather than metric flaws

Severe data limitation: only 10k of 271k MIMIC-CXR samples used for RL Stage 3 due to computational constraints; raises questions about scalability and whether improvements generalize to larger-scale training

Limited clinical evaluation: no human radiologist assessment; reference-based metrics (CheXpert F1, RadGraph F1) don't validate clinical utility; absolute improvements are modest (BLEU-4: 0.136→0.143) despite large percentages; no error analysis or failure case discussion

Insufficient design choice justification: multiple pipeline design decisions (Eq. 9 functional form, validation metric balancing, stage freezing patterns) with limited ablation; hyperparameter sensitivity unclear and dataset-dependent (e.g., entropy coefficient only for IU-Xray)

Poor isolation of pipeline components: three-stage pipeline introduces many confounded variables; only full pipeline variants ablated, not individual design choices; unclear attribution of improvements
Lack of theoretical analysis: no convergence guarantees, no formal justification for why RER/VAPR should work, no analysis of failure modes or boundary conditions
Limited generalization scope: only evaluated on chest X-ray reports; applicability to other medical imaging or general sequence generation tasks unclear; design may be domain-specific
